text:
1. Formula check  
   • All four choices have C₉H₁₁NO₂, so formula alone is not decisive.

2. IR data  
   • 3420  & 3325 cm⁻¹ (two N–H stretches) ⇒ primary –NH₂ present.  
   • 1720 cm⁻¹ strong C=O stretch.  
        – Esters: 1735-1715 cm⁻¹ (conjugation with an aromatic ring lowers it to ≈1720 cm⁻¹).  
        – Primary amides: 1690-1650 cm⁻¹ (too low for 1720 cm⁻¹).  
   → Amide structures (C & D) are inconsistent with the 1720 cm⁻¹ band; an ester is required.  
   → Retain A and B; discard C and D.

3. ¹H NMR data  
   • 1.20 ppm (t, 3 H) and 4.5 ppm (q, 2 H): classic –OCH₂CH₃ (ethyl group attached to oxygen in an ester).  
   • 4.0 ppm (br s, 2 H): –NH₂ protons.  
   • 7.0 ppm (d, 2 H) and 8.0 ppm (d, 2 H): two doublets (AA′BB′), typical of a para-disubstituted benzene ring.

   Comparison of A and B:  
   • In 4-aminophenyl propionate (A) the ethyl group is CH₃CH₂–C(O)–O–Ph.  The CH₂ next to the carbonyl (–CH₂–C=O) would appear near 2.3 ppm, not at 4.5 ppm.  
   • In ethyl 4-aminobenzoate (B) the ethyl group is –OCH₂CH₃; the O-CH₂ resonates at 4.2–4.5 ppm, exactly matching the observed quartet.

Therefore only choice B accounts simultaneously for the IR carbonyl frequency, the two N–H stretches, the O-CH₂ quartet at 4.5 ppm, and the para-disubstituted aromatic pattern.

Answer: B
